I have not the section, but under the old law vessels using internal combustion engines are not subject to inspection. Then why are they brought under this bill? In what way has navigation in Canada been affected by the use of the internal combustion engine? I say the change is not necessary, and I agree with the hon. member for Pietou who the other night strenuously objected to certain of these clauses because of the phraseology. I do not know who drafted them; surely it was not the Prime Minister. Although he looks after nearly all the legislation of this government, he would not use such phrases found in some of those clauses. I say to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Marine that I have no particular objection to the rest of this bill, other than Part H. No one is going to be hurt much by the other parts, as far as I had a chance to study it, but I do say that Part II of this bill should go into dry dock, should be repaired from stem to gudgeon, should be overhauled from truck to keelson. I have no objection to gentlemen learned in the law sitting in in order to draft in proper legal terms the ideas of practical 74726-259S
men who know the cathead from the dogwatch and the glory hole from the lazarette. But I do object to these legal men trying to draft an act without consulting with people who know their business. I suggest to the minister that this bill should stand until next year. Call in Captain Mitchell of Halifax, a practical mariner, call in Captain Lindsay of Vancouver, both of whom have sailed the seas in foreign ships for a great many years, and get their ideas of what is necessary in regard to certificates for foreign voyages. Call in practical men who have sailed the seas in coasters and fishing vessels for many years, captains of freighters, and fishermen either on the Pacific or the Atlantic, men of experience who have sailed for years without certificates, consult with them and you will get a bill of which this government and this parliament will be proud; not a bill which cannot stand the light of day, and of which as I said criticism is already coming in. I have received so much already that I cannot possibly deal with it. I plead with the minister and the government to lot this bill stand so that Part II may be redrafted in order that every man in this country who is interested in shipping or vessels may be protected, and men who earn their living on the sea shall not be ostracised or put in a position where they cannot sail their ships, or young men who want to go to sea will not be discouraged by some fancy educational test which none of them can meet.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have to recognize that my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Duff) has done considerable work in studying this bill. Last week he contended that he had had no time to study it, but I see now that he has perused the whole bill. I fully recognize the experience of my hon. friend in marine matters and I appreciate his knowledge. But as he expressed himself he tended to show that he is the only man-
Oh no, that is not fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -who knows something about marine law.
I object to that, that is not fair; I did not say I was the only one who knew anything about marine matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, I say we can infer from the statement of the hon. member that no one but himself-

I can understand the minister inferring that, because he knows a good deal less than I do.
Canada Shipping Act

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is no doubt about that, but I do not think it was necessary for my hon. friend to make the statement he has just made.
You should not have made the first one.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I would remind my hon. friend that this bill has been studied by experts for over two years; in the Marine department we have the best experts who have been studying it for two years with the assistance of legal advisers. I do not know if my hon. friend has done the same with respect to the amendments he has suggested, but if he drafted them himself I think he will admit it is rather dangerous for a layman to attempt to draft the sections of a bill such as this.
I can assure my hon. friend I had no legal advice, it was purely a matter of common, horse sense.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend says he drafted those amendments himself?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Then I shall proceed with the clauses that stood last week, and I have some amendments to propose which have been studied, and which I think will cover some of the points raised by my hon. friend. I urge my hon. friend to be careful before suggesting amendments drafted without the help of legal advice, because it is a very difficult job even for a legal adviser who has some knowledge and experience in marine matters.
Might I ask my hon. friend what legal gentleman who had any knowledge of marine matters helped to prepare this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The first bill drafted was drafted by my assistant deputy minister and my officials under him with the help of Mr. Martin Griffin, K.C., of Vancouver, one of the outstanding lawyers of the west in marine matters.
But he says he used the paste pot and scissors.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I was in the department and I know what Mr. Griffin did and I know what my officials have done for two years. My officials state that these amendments cannot be accepted, they would not fit the rest of the bill at all.

Why?
{Mr. Duff.]

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: For many reasons.
Could the minister explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We shall see as we come to the various sections.

I have already stated that I did not intend to go any further in my opposition to this bill. I would like very well to have kept my promise in that respect but when I hear the minister say that this bill was prepared by experts with knowledge of legal terms connected with marine matters I must say that if those experts cannot give any better exhibition of their knowledge of marine conditions in different sections of Canada than this bill they never should have undertaken to prepare such a bill. I have no fault to find with the experts in the department over which the minister presides; they are competent in carrying out the duties they have to perform, but when anybody in the Department of Marine or the Department of Fisheries, especially the Department of Marine, will undertake to say that this bill does not do an injustice to the fishing industry of the maritime provinces he does not know what he is talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In what respect?
That is the reason I am now rising-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In what respect?
In every respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Tell this committee in what respect.

A few days ago I told the minister and this committee that there were sections which could be amended by the hon. member -for Antigonish-Guysbor-ough or by myself. We could suggest amendments to some of those sections, but there were other sections which we knew were working injustices but which we would not dare, even with our knowledge -of the fishing industry, to undertake to amend without first having the opportunity to -consult the people interested. That is the reason I have asked for delay in the passage of this bill; that is the reason I haive asked the government if they are determined to force it through, and whether or not they would not delay, for this session at least, bringing into operation the first part of the bill. They have authority under one section of the bill to take that action. I received no satisfactory answer to my request, nor did I receive any guarantee that tha-t would be done.

Canada Shipping Act
I agree with the statement of the minister as to the preparation of amendments without the help of legal talent. However, the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough did not suggest that no lawyer should be called in. As a matter of fact he said he had no objection to legal minds being consulted so that the suggested amendments might be framed in proper legal phraseology. He knows that neither he nor I is in a position to place the suggested amendments into proper legal language without first having the cooperation of legal minds. Therefore we are not suggesting that the amendments should be accepted in the exact terms in which they now appear; all we want is to have an acceptance of the subject matter of the amendments. These suggestions come from men who know what the conditions really are, and they know that if the bill passes in its present form it will operate not to the advantage of, but rather to the disadvantage of, the fishing and freighting industries of the maritime provinces. That is the reason we are opposing the bill, and that is the reason I have risen in my place to-day to ask that the passage of the bill be postponed. No interests would suffer. Give us an opportunity t.o consult our people, to lay the whole matter before them, and to come back next year bringing with us suggestions to meet the conditions. In that way the bill could be put through in a proper manner. If any interests might suffer by the nonadoption a.t this session of the bill now under discussion I would hold my tongue, but I say to the minister-and he knows it-that if action on the bill were postponed no interest would suffer. If the government are determined to put the bill through in its present form, then I ask them to take advantage of the power they have under the bill whereby they may not bring into effect those sections affecting coastal freighting and fishing interests of the maritime provinces and the Pacific coast. Do not bring them into operation, but let them stand under the old act until such time as we may consult our people and, coming back here next year as their representatives, lay our opinions before the House of Commons.

Mr. Chairman, after the unparalleled latitude you have allowed other members in this discussion-unparalleled in my experience, at any rate-I presume you will extend to me the same opportunity to wander all over the bill.
I am not surprised that the absurdities and contradictions in the bill have led the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) to depart from the decision he made a few days ago to wash his hands of all responsibility, to let the government put the bill through the house, and to leave them wholly responsible for if. I wholly agreed with that stand, and I proposed to follow it. However, as he and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) have departed from that decision I shall fallow their example, and speak for but a short time indeed, to place on record a wire I received yesterday.
I agreed with hon. members who took the stand that it was hopeless to try to amend this bill, due to the extended and intricate nature of the sections, the wide variety of subjects covered, and the basic fact that the government, without any reasonable excuse so far as I could see, refused to send the bill to a committee where we could have sat around a table, had the advantage of legal experts and technical experts about whom the minister has been talking-an advantage which we certainly would have required-and we would have heard the arguments and settled the matter.
The idea that a layman cannot formulate an amendment is pure nonsense. The committee could function, and could decide along laymen's lines what they wanted done. The committee would adjourn, and the lawyer in the department could be present to draft appropriate amendments for the next sitting, when he would find whether or not the amendments agreed with the ideas in the minds of the members. That has been done scores of times, and it is useless to suggest that it could not be done again. I remember sitting on a committee which framed the old age pensions legislation. I believe there were only four of us, and a lawyer. Within certain limits indicated by the government, he would ask us what we wanted, draft the section and bring it down next day. That legislation although a new departure, stood the test of a great deal of criticism until the present government messed it up with a lot of ill-timed regulations.
With a great deal of what the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has said, I agree. With some of his statements perhaps I might not agree. With a good deal of what he has said I do not know whether I can agree or not, because I simply do not know about all those matters. I am quite appreciative of the fact, however, that he does know about these matters, and that on a committee his presence and knowledge would be of great value in arranging the details of various sections. But the minister has no intention of sending the bill to a committee, and never
Canada Shipping Act

had. He has no intention of leaving it for another year, and never had. What is the use of wasting time urging him to do so? I do not purpose wasting either my time or that of the committee.
The minister has said he will now introduce some amendments. That is remarkable when we recall his remarks upon the introduction of the bill and upon second reading. In his view the shipping bill was the last word in legislation and could not possibly be improved upon. I was reminded of Moses going up to the mountain and coming down with the ten commandments.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I stated as a whole
it is a remarkable piece of legislation.

It is a remarkable bill, all right; I admit that, and I suggest that time will demonstrate how remarkable it really is. We will be sitting here next session-those of us who are fortunate enough to return-and we will be amending this bill. However I am not going to waste the time of the committee by any further observations, but shall proceed to quote the telegram I have before me. Hansard indicates-and if the minister wishes I shall quote it-that he said that a committee sitting in another place heard all people interested in this matter. In fact, I think the Salvation Army was about the only body which was not heard. If there was anybodj'' or anything which had an interest in the bill, it was heard. Then, later on in reply to a question put by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) we find the minister stating that the seamen from Vancouver had not been heard. At a later point he admitted they had not been heard, but said they had presented a brief. Still later that statement was contradicted. At a later point he referred to telegrams, but notwithstanding the request of an hon. member on this side of the house to read those telegrams, he did not do so. He apparently read selected excerpts which gave the impression in one case that the whole engineering bodies of Canada were behind it, but upon being pressed by the hon. member for Hamilton we found that it was only one-seventeenth of those bodies, only one council out of seventeen, which is a very different thing.
I just want to quote a wire that I have received from an important body in Vancouver, the Canadian Merchant Service Guild of Vancouver, which the minister said had been fully heard. It is a long wire and I am pleased to say that it was not sent collect. It; is addressed to myself and reads as follows:

Hansard eight June. Received on the sixteenth; thanks. Your statements properly taken but nominal horse power only one reason-[DOT]
By the reference to nominal horsepower they are no doubt referring to the quotation I made with reference to someone who wanted a change in the nominal horsepower.
-only one reason why practical and honest advice should be secured before passing Bill E.
That is not my sentiment; it is the sentiment of this body interested only in their own affairs, and they say that practical and honest advice should be secured before passing this bill:
Example: Two vessels identical motor engines quoted in registry shipping Shean eighty-four and Czar eighteen nominal.
The telegram goes on:
Majority vessels now driven motor engines defined by makers and users brake horse power but no provision for such made in act being another proof act is already fifteen years obsolete and impractical in many respects.
They say that we are fifteen years behind the times as regards the proposed bill itself. The telegram continues:
Please concentrate on elimination subsections (b) and two of section one twenty, being rank discrimination against coasting inland and minor water masters and mates who have upheld the highest traditions of the sea.
That is the section that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough quoted in connection with the qualifications of officers.
Such legislation can serve no good purpose except to satisfy some childish whim or prejudice and would destroy that higher statutes-
I think "standing" is meant:
-which the proponents of the act apparently do not understand. Please endeavour have coasting limits not less than ten south instead of thirty-six north to permit Canadian officers and ships to trade between eastern and western Canada ports through Panama canal. Copy our brief mailed Minister Marine and Senate twelfth April will reach you Wednesday. Meantime use this telegram as required.
Canadian Merchant Service Guild.
If that last sentence had not been there I would have hesitated to put that somewhat drastic criticism on Hansard, but they are apparently quite willing that it should be so used. This brief was mailed to the minister. It is the first I have heard of it. Did it reach the Senate committee? We do not know. The committee did not print its evidence. The minister is going to say, "Yes, it was submitted." I have no doubt it was and that the only consideration it received was whether it should be pigeonholed under the letter "C" or the letter "G," being the

Canada Shipping Act
first letter of the name of the man perhaps or of the association. We have no record before us that the brief was considered. We have only the minister's statement that it was ever received at all. Certainly it was not considered by any member of this house. At any rate this substantial and important representative body of seamen are, to put it mildly, very far from satisfied with this bill when they talk about its needing practical and honest advice. The act is fifteen years obsolete in its wording, they say, and impractical in many respects. Certainly the statements that we have heard from the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough do bear out, so far as my limited knowledge goes, much of what they say.
I turn to section 120. That is the section dealing with certificates not valid. It says that these certificates will not be valid after a period of five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
allow me? I am sorry that my hon. friends have not allowed the minister to proceed with the amendments he was to propose to the committee. I have an amendment here to strike out that subsection limiting the life of a certificate to five years, and I am going to ask the committee to consent to another provision giving the minister the power to make an inquiry and set aside a certificate if the certificated mariner is found upon investigation to be incapable of performing his duties and still persists in following his calling when he has a life certificate.

I am very glad indeed to
hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
As to the nominal
horsepower question, there will be a definition of "sailing" vessel proposed when we come to the section but may I say here that nominal horsepower is the standard way of calculating the power of an engine all over the empire, and we felt it was better to follow the standard way throughout the empire rather than have a way of our own.

I am pleased indeed to hear
what the minister says.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend
understands that it is only for legal purposes, because it is well known that one nominal horsepower means about twenty brake horsepower, or rather the reverse, twenty brake horsepower means one nominal horsepower.

The "break" just made by
the minister indicates his ignorance as well as my own in regard to these technical matters. I am very glad indeed to hear that the minister is going to make these changes. It indicates the advisability of adhering to the ordinary rules and going through this bill section by section instead of allowing us to talk all over the lot as we have been doing. Apparently, according to the terms of this wire, it is the custom for motor driven engines to be described by the makers and users in terms of brake horsepower, not of course steam engines, and that is what these people are referring to. I am quite willing to wait until the different sections come up to hear the amendments the minister has to propose, but that again illustrates the extreme advisability of sending this bill to a special committee where these questions could have been argued out. The Canadian Merchant Service Guild sent their brief to the minister on the twelfth of April, making their suggestions, and now the minister tells us that he has amendments to move. Why not have put them in the bill in the first place? I think that in the other chamber there has been a complete lack of a proper understanding of the subject they were dealing with, or they have ignored the representations that have been made by these people. If their representations are to be given effect to now, why were they not given effect to in April? I am glad that the changes are being made but I do not believe that they will be sufficient to make the whole bill workable, and I do not propose to take any responsibility for this bill. Let the government pass this bill if they wish, and let them take the responsibility. If there are to be any changes, I shall be glad to hear them when we come to the various sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am sorry my hon.
friends are making general statements about this bill, and trying to show that very important changes are being made in the existing law. I should like to put on record a comparison of the present law and section 113 of this bill, to show that there is practically no change in the exemptions.
Why not simplify the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Section 113 of the
present bill requires that every ship except those mentioned in paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) shall have certificated masters. Section 93 of the Canada Shipping Act provides:
No ship registered in Canada, over one hundred tons registered tonnage, shall go to sea from any port or place in Canada on any voyage not being a coasting voyage, unless the master and first mate or only mate thereof have obtained and possess valid certificates.

Canada Shipping Act
Section 94 requires that every sailing ship registered in Canada of over 150 tons registered tonnage, and every steamship when employed in the coasting trade or plying on any Canadian water, shall have a certificated master. The act provides for certain exemptions under section 98. What are those exemptions? Under the Canada Shipping Act, the first exemption is for pleasure yachts. There is the same exemption in this bill.
Why exempt pleasure boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am only making a
comparison between the present act and this bill.
That does not do any good.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The next exemption in the bill is for ships solely employed in fishing. The exemption in the existing act is for ships employed solely in fishing. The next exemption in the act is for steamships of not more than five tons gross tonnage. The exemptions in the bill are for passenger steamships not exceeding five tons gross tonnage and steamships not carrying passengers and not exceeding ten tons gross tonnage.

Did the minister ever see a
steamship of five tons gross register?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am only making
a comparison. My hon. friend has stated that this bill is entirely different from the existing law as far as certificated masters are concerned, and I am attempting to show that that is not the case.
It is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The next exemption
in the existing act is for barges or other vessels having neither masts, sails nor rigging, and not being steamships. The exemption in the bill is for barges or other vessels having neither masts, sails nor rigging, and not being steamships-exactly the same thing. The next exemption in the existing act is for "sailing ships engaged in the coastwise trade of not more than one hundred tons, registered tonnage, propelled by auxiliary power other than steam, employed partly in fishing and partly in the carriage of freight." The exemption in this bill is for "home-trade, inland waters or minor waters sailing ships not exceeding one hundred and fifty tons register tonnage." I have an amendment to suggest to the definition of "sailing vessels" which will help the situation. As a matter of fact, the exemptions in this bill are perhaps greater than they are under the existing law.

No.
(Mr. Duranleau.]

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: With reference to the difference between a foreign and home-trade voyage. The bill defines an inland voyage, a minor waters voyage and a home-trade voyage. Is it not sufficient to say that a foreign voyage is one outside of those three definitions? As I said before, the difference between a foreign and a home-trade voyage is not based on geography, it is based on the hazards of navigation. The same principle is applied all over the empire.

Let me say to the minister
that the hazards of navigation are not nearly as great on a foreign voyage as they are on a home-trade voyage.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The hon. member has made his statement and I would ask him not to interrupt. He stated a moment ago that there was not the same rule in England, but I claim that exactly the same principle applies there. The definition of a home-trade voyage in the Merchant Shipping Act would cover, for instance, certain voyages from England to Germany or France where there are no great dangers or hazards. A voyage from Vancouver to Montreal would be a "foreign voyage" on account of the hazards of navigation, because it would necessitate a ship having to take the deep seas before reaching the Panama canal, in which case the hazards of navigation would be greater.
No, they are not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Such a ship leaving
Vancouver would have to go more than two hundred miles from the coast, it would have to pass through the Panama canal, up the Atlantic coast and then up the St. Lawrence to Montreal. The experts claim that such voyages should be made only by ships having sufficient strength to make a deep-sea voyage and carrying the same life saving apparatus and the same certificated master. These rules are for the protection of life at sea and I think my hon. friends are wrong when they want to define a home-trade voyage as one between two ports in Canada. I should like to proceed with the sections which have not yet been adopted and if my hon. friends have any suggestions to make, I shall be glad to hear them.

What does the Canada
Shipping Act give as the definition of steamship?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That is given in section 73, subsection (i) and reads:
"Steamship" or "steamer" includes any ship propelled wholly or in part by steam or motive power other than sail or oars.

Canada Shipping Act

That is not the same as
the definition given in this bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It means the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Subsection 101 of
section 2 of the bill reads:
"Steamship" or "steamer" (except as may be provided under the load line rules) means any shiip propelled by machinery, and not coming within the definition of sailing ship.
I am not an expert in this matter, but I think my officials know something about it, and they assure me that there is no difference between the two.

Under definition 89 a sailing ship is described as so and so, and when you come to the last part of subsection 89 you find the following:
and which, in addition, is provided with mechanical means of propulsion, the power of which does not exceed three nominal horse power.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
In this regard I have another definition to propose:
"Sailing ship" (except as may be provided under the load line rules) means a ship propelled wholly by sails, and includes a ship not in excess of 150 tons, gross tonnage, provided with masts, sails and rigging sufficient to allow her to make voyages under sail alone, and which, in addition, is provided with mechanical means of propulsion other than a steam engine.
I think this definition will cover the whole point.
Then you will have to change the definition of 101.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Why?
Because the moment you depart from rigging, under 89, and insert a certain horse power, even if she is under 150 tons, she becomes a steamship.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Definition 101 states very clearly that the vessel shall not come within the definition of sailing ship.
Under the present definition, 89, if she has a nominal horse power of over three horse power she becomes a steamer and is no longer a sailing ship.

The minister has read some of the sections and has pointed out that there is little difference between the old act and the new. I understand that the old definition of a home-trade vessel was divided into three parts, but under the present provision there are only two definitions. Heretofore a boat could leave Montreal or Vancouver for Buenos Aires provided it did not cross the ocean; it would then be a h'ome-trade voyage. But under the present definition of home-trade voyage no boat will be allowed to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at the existing act he will see that the definition of home-trade ship refers only to the signing of seamen.

Under the old act the definition of home trade voyage would allow a ship to leave Vancouver, New Westminster or Montreal and go to Buenos Aires provided it did not directly cross the ocean. Now, by the new definition, a home-trade vessel though it may operate twenty or thirty or even more miles out from the shore, will not be allowed to leave Vancouver and go to Montreal, say, with lumber or any other cargo. As regards hazards at sea, there is just as much hazard leaving New Westminster or Vancouver and going to Los Angeles or Panama as there is in going through the Panama canal and coming up the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The definition of home trade under the existing act refers only to the engagement of seamen. Section 124, subsection (c) reads:
"Canadian home trade ship" includes every ship registered in either of the provinces, employed in trading or going from any place or places in any of the provinces to any other place or places in any other of the provinces.
What is the definition of coastal trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: This definition is included in part III, which deals with seamen only.

I must come back to this point, because it will affect ships leaving either the Atlantic or the Pacific coast for ports in Canada, I cannot accept the minister's statement in regard to hazards, because there is just as much hazard going to the Queen Charlotte islands and other places as there is crossing the Atlantic. A man has to be a real sailor to go to Queen Charlotte islands. There is just as much hazard going from New Westminster to Los Angeles-I believe they go seventy-five miles from shore-as there is coming up on the other side, and I see no reason why going through the Panama and coming up the other side of Montreal should bring a vessel within the classification of foreign and not home trade voyages.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If my hon. friend will compare the existing act with this bill he will find that while there may be a difference as to certificated masters, there is no change as regards the strength and structure of ships.

There is quite a difference. The minister read clauses from the Shipping Act to bear out his contention, and I say that he
Canada Shipping Act

is failing to take into account one most important feature that has a bearing on Canadian ships.

I thought I made it clear that under chapter 186, the old act, instead of being called home trade voyage it was called coastal voyage, and I read to the committee the definition of coastal voyage, which extended to 40 south latitude. That goes as far south as Buenos Aires. The minister says that is not correct, and I would ask him to have his officials look it up; I forget just now what the section is.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not think I said what the hon. member stated.

The minister said that the
old act was not any broader than this. I say that under the old act instead of being a home trade voyage, it was a coastal voyage, something every sailor could understand, and it extended to Buenos Aires. That would take in what my hon. friend said. In order to meet the minister's views I was willing to bring it up to five degrees north latitude which would be in the latitude of British Guiana where the Canadian National steamships, the ships of the Minister of Railways, go every fortnight. Surely that is a fair compromise. The minister says that a home trade voyage is the same under the old act as it is under this. What does he say besides that? The minister will not say that I am trying to be too critical with him. He says that foreign voyages are more hazardous than home trade or coastal voyages. I do not know who advised the minister, but let me say that the worst voyage a vessel can make is from the bay of Fundy through Long Island Sound to New York. I would rather cross the Atlantic ten times than go from the bay of Fundy to Boston or New York, and yet that is a home trade voyage. Still the minister tries to tell the committee that a foreign voyage is more hazardous than a home trade voyage. Surely somebody is misleading him. I do not want to waste my time here; I desire to go home and to do some business, but I say to the minister he should move that the committee rise because he has been badly advised by his officials when he says to any intelligent man not only on the floor of the house but elsewhere that a foreign voyage is more hazardous than a home trade voyage. That is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That is not what I
said.

The minister said that a
foreign voyage was more hazardous than a 
home trade voyage. A home trade voyage is ten times as hazardous. Did the minister ever leave Halifax and go to Canso or leave Vancouver and go up the inside channel to Prince Rupert? I would rather leave Vancouver and go to Hongkong than go to Prince Rupert. Let us get down to brass tacks. How are we going to trust our officials if we are going to be told tommyrot like this? I do not want to be too critical; I do not want to say that the minister does not know anything about the bill, but what I have said shows conclusively that the bill should stand. It was considered for two years in the Senate.
Order. We are dealing with subclause 26 of clause 2.

I am dealing with foreign
voyages.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
observations are wholly foreign to the clause.

Well, I have heard the Prime Minister in previous remarks just as far away from the point as a home trade voyage would be under this clause. Instead of subclause 26 with which we are dealing and the strange amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion), I made a suggestion to the minister before the Prime Minister came in and I believe he will agree with me in his heart if he does not outwardly.
I said that subclause 26 instead of reading as it does should read in this way, and I will read it so that the Prime Minister may hear me. I will first read what it says in this wonderful bill which came from another place:
"Foreign voyage" means either a voyage between a place in Canada-
That might mean up in lake Winnipeg, for instance.
-and a place not in Canada-
That might mean anywhere else.
-other than a place within the limits of a home trade voyage or a voyage between places not in Canada and not all within the limits of a home trade voyage.
Did the committee ever hear such a stupid, ridiculous definition as that? That clause alone cost the country some $10,000 with those wonderful legal men who, the minister told us, drafted this bill. Then the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, which is far removed from the stormy waters of the Atlantic or the Pacific, moved the following amendment to this subclause:
"Foreign voyage" means a voyage extending beyond the area of a home trade voyage


Canada Shipping Act
Where else would it be? This is taken., for granted.
-and not being an inland voyage or a minor waters voyage.
Is that not a great suggestion coming from the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency? Before the Prime Minister came in, I did not move but I suggested that subclause 2 of clause 2 be amended to read:
"Foreign voyage"-
I am delighted to see the Prime Minister in his seat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am bound to say that
he is not listening to the hon. gentleman.
Is it nice to say that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is nice to say that.

This is what I suggested:
"Foreign voyage" means a voyage between Canada, and a port east of the 60th degree of longitude and south of the fifth degree north latitude, and north of the 65th degree-*
That is on the Atlantic coast.
-and a port west of the 125th degree of longitude, and south of the fifth degree north latitude, and north of the 65th degree.
There I have given a simple amendment in nautical terms which every sailor, every mariner, understands, and not a clause like the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency nor like what was in the bill which the Prime Minister said must go through this house this session in spite of the fact that it came down here only a few days ago. That is a simple suggestion to clear up the matter. If I were playing politics I would say: Let the bill go through; there would not be a mariner or a sailor or a business man vote for the government at the next election if this bill goes on the statute books. But the matter is too serious for that; there are thousands of men interested in shipping and all I am trying to do is straighten out certain clauses which I have had time to consider so that the bill will be reasonable and clear and will not be a conglomeration of pastepot and scissors as it is as drafted by the legal gentleman who spent two years in preparing it.

I would call the hon. member to
order again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
referred to me and therefore I think it well for me to say how clearly the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency indicates what is desired. There are three kinds of voyages; home voyage, foreign voyage, inland voyage. The
home voyage is defined in the statute and the amendment moved makes it clear that it is any voyage other than a foreign voyage or an inland voyage.
Or a minor waters voyage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Can one get anything
clearer than that?
It is as clear as mud.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
By excluding the other
named voyages, necessarily the term "home voyage" includes all other forms of voyages. Could anything be clearer than that? Instead of fixing it by latitude and longitude, you fix it by the form of voyage, and all forms of voyages which a ship may take other than those named as excepted shall be home voyages. Does the committee wish anything clearer than that?

I would think we would deal with the foreign voyage first and then necessarily use those terms outside of the foreign voyage. The minister has got it all twisted; he is going backwards; he has reversed his engines and is going back half speed. I say the foreign voyage should be the voyage designated. I also say that if the Prime Minister's statement is right a man who wants to make a foreign voyage has to look up this act and see what a home-trade voyage means and then what an inland voyage means and what a minor waters voyage means. So that before he gets through he will be trying to get up the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa river over the mountains and the Lord knows where he will get. Why not put it in simple language that a sailor can understand? Why all this nonsense about other than a home trade and inland water voyage? Who ever heard of such ridiculous nonsense in a definition?
Mr. DURAN'LEAU:	In defining these
different kinds of voyages we are proceeding in the way vchich has been adopted by England for centuries. If you look at the Merchant Shipping Act you will see that England defines a minor waters voyage, an inland waters voyage, a home-trade voyage and a foreign voyage. In England the home-trade voyage includes all kinds of small voyages, on inland or minor waters-all are included in home-trade voyages-and then the others are the foreign voyages. In this bill we have minor waters voyages; inland waters voyages and home-trade voyages defined very clearly. Then we say all other voyages will be foreign voyages. I think that is clear.

My hon. friend said a moment ago that the English act defines minor voyages
Canada Shipping Act

and so on, and a moment afterwards he turned right around, went on another tack and said the only thing in the English act was home-trade and foreign voyages. If the minister is going to change his views in even half a second on this thing how can we expect him to know much about the other sections? He told us deliberately a moment ago that in the British act there were minor waters voyages and inland waters and home-trade voyages, and because he realized he made a mistake he turned around and said, No, pardon me, there are two definitions in England, home-trade and foreign. That is the trouble with this whole bill; the minister has not studied it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Mr. Smith, Cumberland) : Order.
What is wrong with that?
Everything is wrong. We are on subsection 26.
We are talking about voyages. I am quite in order.

In order to have some understanding about a foreign voyage one must know the line of division between interior and exterior waters, especially in the St. Lawrence river. For a long time I have been asking the government what is the line of division between interior and exterior waters in the St. Lawrence river. I was told that no change had been made. I understand that the "exterior" waters come like a V in the gulf of St. Lawrence and river St. Lawrence. I would like to know from the minister what the line of demarcation is.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I would draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that in the bill there is no definition of interior or exterior waters; the terms used are "inland waters of Canada," and they are defined in subsection 41 of section 2:
_ "Inland waters of Canada" means all the rivers, lakes and other navigable fresh waters within Canada, and includes the river St. Lawrence as far seaward as a line drawn from Father Point to Point Orient.

Yes, but the Royal Canadian Mounted Police gave certain instructions to their men some time ago, and I asked the government why there was a change. Instructions were given first for the men of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to stay within a certain line. Afterwards other instructions were given, and then new instructions were given in accordance with the first instructions. I would ask the minister why that line has been changed, and at whose request.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not think there is any change in the law as to that line. I understand my hon. friend means in the St. Lawrence river. I think it was the same line before, from Father Point to Point Orient. I have no knowledge of any instructions given to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as to the limits of our inland waters. If my hon. friend refers to a special case I shall be pleased to have the particulars and to investigate it, but I do not think there was any change in regard to the limits of our inland waters in the St. Lawrence.

I shall not insist any further at the moment. I will take it up at eight o'clock and see in Hansard the precise answer given by the government. The point is I could not get any information about the change in the line dividing interior and exterior waters, but what I know is that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have given instructions to their men which were entirely different from former instructions, and I wondered what was the reason for that change. If there is a line it cannot be changed at the will of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If that line is good for the merchant marine it is good as well for the police. Navigation within that line is inland shipping, and outside of it is foreign shipping. Therefore it is a most important line of demarcation, and we are entitled to have all available information about it. It is of the utmost importance because when the ships go outside of that line they are no longer under the jurisdiction of Canada; they are sailing under international law. Therefore it is most important to have that information. I shall be more precise about it at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, previous to passing the two sections 338 and 339, I wish to make a few comments. At page 47, French version, of a report tabled in the house, Sir Alexander Gibb expresses himself as follows:
The existence of good pilots is of profound importance to Canada, and particularly on the St. Lawrence route, which has only with difficulty been established as one of the great highways of shipping. The Department of Marine has devoted a great amount of thought to the lighting and buoying arrangements and other aids to navigation-and with outstanding success. It is essential, therefore, that the pilotage also should be closely controlled by government.
From the evidence I obtained, it is clear that the standard of St. Lawrence pilots is, on the whole, high; and the administration of this branch of the Department of Marine has a reputation for strictness.
Under the former act ships coming from the province of Ontario and having to go down the St. Lawrence river from Montreal to Quebec and from Quebec to Father Point were obliged to provide themselves with pilots. According to the new act under consideration, pilotage service will not be required between Quebec and Father Point. I contend, sir, that the pilotage between Quebec and Father Point is as dangerous and difficult as that between Montreal and Quebec, in connection with coastal navigation.
Navigation between Quebec and Father Point can only be guided by compass, or by beams of light cast from lighthouses located along the coast. Often, if not generally, fog prevails in the lower St. Lawrence river, so that navigation is very difficult. If navigators, without any previous experience, are permitted to navigate the lower St. Lawrence river without a pilot's licence, navigation in those waters will become difficult. I fear, especially, that when this bill has been sanctioned, such as it is drafted, we shall have acicdents. Moreover, the past has shown that many accidents which happen in the lower St. Lawrence river, could be traced to the fact that certain vessels were not provided with men possessing the required qualifications to pilot them.
Pilots are required to possess particularly those from the lower St. Lawrence river between Quebec and Father Point, special qualifications and the navigation regulations in connection with the pilotage of those waters are entirely different from those required from persons who navigate on the Great Lakes or between Quebec and Montreal.
I again state, that special qualifications are required for pilots of the Quebec district.
They must be acquainted with the rules governing ocean navigation and a more thorough knowledge of navigation is expected from them than from those who navigate the Great Lakes. Therefore, if this bill is passed in its present form, we shall have navigators without any knowledge of the lower St. Lawrence river, not having passed any test required from pilots, and such persons will be placed in charge of vessels who will have to meet, to pass or be passed by other vessels in charge of experienced seamen who were obliged to pass difficult tests.
I submit, sir, that the Quebec section should be placed on same footing as that of the Montreal section. Namely, vessels which navigate along the coast between Quebec and Father Point should be placed on the same footing as those navigating between Montreal and Quebec. I am not a sailor myself, however, from what I have heard, I gather that navigation is more difficult between Quebec and Father Point than between Quebec and Montreal. Between the latter two places, the channel is very narrow, but it is lighted day and night, it is so to speak buoyed throughout, while the Channel between Quebec and Father Point does not possess the same advantages. Moreover, between Quebec and Father Point, it very often happens that vessels are obliged to anchor and wait for the high tide. If navigators who have no experience of the lower St. Lawrence river are permitted to meet and pass vessels provided with pilots, it is clear that accidents will happen. For the good name of that part of the St. Lawrence river, we should place the section between Quebec and Father Point on the same footing as that between Quebec and Montreal and we should therefore add the word "Quebec" after the word "Montreal" in sections 338 and 339, in order that seamen who may have to navigate the lower St. Lawrence river will have no fear of meeting vessels in charge of persons who have had no experience of these waters.

Mr. Chairman, I do not always have an opportunity of agreeing with the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion). However, I

Canada Shipping Act

think that many of his suggestions, this evening, should appeal to the house. I have had a little experience in this connection- perhaps not as much as some, however, I have acquired a little since I represent in this house a maritime county. A number of representations have been made to me, with reference to section 338, by pilots who have had a wide experience, especially, by those who are required to pilot ships between Que-ber and the lower St. Lawrence. These pilots wish to be granted the same advantages and privileges as those of the Montreal district. I think that an amendment to that effect was moved in the Senate.
I deem it my duty to bring to the attention of the house an excerpt of a letter, dated May 31, 1934, from Mr. Cyrille Pouliot, special pilot for the Cunard line:
I request to oppose with the greatest energy and vigour section 338, clause (id) which grants certain unwarranted exemptions, as they will be the source of most severe accidents and, unfortunately, with loss of life. I have included in this letter a list of a number of accidents which took place in our section when no pilots were on board such vessels.
Those are, I think, the accidents to which my colleague for Quebee-Montmorency referred, a few moments ago. Such, for instance, the accident to the Empress of Ireland; in 1914, five miles outside the pilotage limits, at Father Point, the collision occurred with the ss. Storstad and 900 lives were lost. There was no pilot on board. Take the case of the General Wolfe vessel, in 1910, which was sunk at Murray Bay when a collision occurred with the ship Arranmore. No pilot was on board. Loss of life. Has not been refloated.
It was decided, about 1917, that colliers of the merchant marine plying between Sidney and Quebec would take no more pilots on board and that the captain would himself steer his ship. Hardly had such a decision been taken that the ss. Warrior grounded at the "St. Roch crossing." The same night, the Canadian Recruit which had no pilot on board was sunk by the Maskinonge in the Patch channel. The wreck remained there, and later a C.P.R. steamship tore its hull on it. This wreck having become an obstruction and a constant danger, the government expended very large amounts to remove it.
There is also the case of the steamship Montmagnv. This government vessel collided on September 18, 1914, with the ss. Lengham, in the de Beaujeu channel. The ship was proceeding down the channel on the wrong side. It tried to cross over but was struck and sunk by the Lengham. Its hull is still
rMr. Casgrain.]
there. There was a loss of life. No pilot was on board.
A tug was sunk by the ss. Batiscan at Madame island, in 1914. It was on the wrong side of the channel and when it tried to cross over, it was struck and sunk. This time again we had to deplore the loss of life. No pilot was on board.
The Christine, another vessel, was sunk by a submarine at Saint-Jean, Island of Orleans. Its hull which is an obstruction, still rests in the same place. There was one loss of life in this accident. No pilot was on board.
There is also the case of another ship, the Hochelaga. In 1926, this vessel of the Dominion Coal Co., was proceeding up the river on the wrong side of the channel without a pilot. It suddenly tried to cross over and was struck by the vessel Leopold D. The Hochelaga was blamed for this accident by a decision of the admiralty court.
There are other cases of like disasters and a more complete list could be given, if necessary. I think these are sound reasons to prove that the privileges granted to the pilots of the Montreal district should also be granted to those of the Quebec district. I shall not quote all the comments which were made to me as regards the reasons in favour of granting these advantages to the pilots of the Quebec district. I simply wish to quote the conclusion arrived at by Mr. Cyrille Pouliot, who is a regularly appointed pilot of the Cunard line. I am personally acquainted with him, he is a very efficient man in his profession, that is why I take the liberty of submitting to the committee his views. He states:
If this Bill E passes, we, the pilots, can no further guarantee the safety of vessels as against the danger of collisions.
We shall, perhaps, be obliged, at times, to ground our own vessels, in order to protect life. If it is intended to repeat the disaster of the Empress of Ireland with its 900 losses of life, it is only necessary to adopt this bill E. The government will not be able to contend that it was not warned by practical men.
We have but to let the bill pass in its present form and allow the vessels coming from the great lakes, Sidney or elsewhere, to proceed to Quebec, without the services of pilots and the unfortunate accidents such as those I quoted will reoccur.
Certain arguments are put forth by people who contend that it is unnecessary to have pilots. They are generally put forth by captains in charge of vessels coming from the Great Lakes and, while on their way to Montreal, take a rest when going through the canal. They have the services of pilots when

Canada Shipping Act
proceeding from Montreal to Quebec and, arriving at Quebec, they contend that they can easily steer their vessels to and fro in the lower St. Lawrence. They argue that after a number of trips, having already had the assistance of pilots, they have a sufficient knowledge of the routes and ports to enable them to dock at Clark city, Shelby or other similar ports, with the same facility as pilots. As I have just shown in my remarks in connection with the various accidents that have occurred-and as the hon. member for Que-bec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion) also stated- in certain cases when it is a matter of steering in one direction or of leaving one of these ports below Quebec so as to proceed to the open sea, it becomes much more difficult for a captain whatever may be his qualifications or his efficiency or his acquired skillfulness, he is exposed to all the dangers of meeting vessels or ships coming from the high sea.
When responsible and large companies take advantage on each trip of the services of pilots so as to protect the life of citizens and the goods they carry, it is only just that other companies, who carry on coastal trade and make use of the river route, be tied down to the same regulations.
There is another question. If other unfortunate accidents happen owing to the fact that no steps were taken to compel these companies to take on pilots below Quebec, I think that insurance companies will increase their rates and this in the long run will rather be detrimental to the various companies instead of being beneficial to them. There would be no harm done, sir, in granting to pilots of the Quebec district and those below Quebec, the same privileges as enjoyed by pilots between Montreal and Quebec. I think that this is necessary and that we should insist that these vessels which proceed from Montreal to Quebec and vice versa, and those that navigate between Quebec and the ports on the northern coast and also as far as Father Point, should have a pilot on board.
I am aware that such an amendment was moved in the Senate and discussed. It is unfortunate that it was not adopted. I do not think that it has any chance of passing this-house, because generally when a bill comes from the Senate it is passed such as it is. It would be better to reconsider such a decision. The question is sufficiently important to reconsider it from the viewpoint of safety and protection to life, in case of accidents.

I generally agree with my deskmate (Mr. Casgrain) and I should like to agree with the very moderate presentation which he and the hon. member who preceded him have made of this case. But I venture 74726 -260J
to say that their submission only shows that when one concession is made it leads to another. We have never had compulsory pilotage between Quebec and Montreal. This bill provides that there shall be compulsory pilotage between those ports. That is a considerable hardship on shipping, particularly the shipping of the part of the dominion from which I come, operating up the St. Lawrence. Now having obtained that, my hon. friends- and I do not blame them; they present the views of those who have made representations to them-now propose that shipping shall have an additional burden placed upon it by having pilotage made compulsory below Quebec. Never since confederation, and that is quite a long time, has there been a compulsory provision affecting the lower portion of the river. Perhaps my hon. friends do not realize what a heavy burden they seek to impose on shipping, and particularly on the products of the province of Nova Scotia. I speak especially of the coal trade. I know one company which has eighteen vessels, which make an average of about twenty trips a year; this means 720 trips back and forth between Quebec and Father Point.

speechtext: What company?

Dominion Coal Company. It would mean the imposing of a $65,000 burden on the Nova Scotia coal trade if compulsory pilotage were enacted applying to the pilotage district below Quebec. That is a substantial handicap. The government is endeavouring to assist in the marketing of Nova Scotia coal in central Canada by affording subsidies in connection with transportation, and it seems to me that if compulsory pilotage were imposed it would be giving with one hand and taking away with the other. While my hon. friends are perfectly justified in presenting the cases of the men whom they represent, at the same time we must remember that the trade of this country should have some consideration as well. Not since confederation have we had compulsory pilotage there, and as we all know that the route is being improved constantly, it seems to me that the argument for compulsory pilotage between Quebec and the mouth of the river is getting weaker all the time.
Further let me point out that the next section, 339, is rather ominous. As one who wants to see the coal trade of Nova Scotia developed I must say that I have some apprehension in regard to that section, which provides that the pilotage authority may make the pilotage district below Quebec compulsory. That threat is always hanging over
Canada Shipping Act

the Nova Scotia coal trade. My hon. friend has suggested that it is safer to take pilots. I do not know anything about these matters except what I am told, but I understand that below Quebec there are only two dredged channels and that they constitute a very small portion of the route, and outside of that it is open water. The suggestion is made that currents and fog are encountered, but I submit that the masters of our vessels are quite as competent and have as much experience with currents and fog as any pilots they could get, with all respect to the gentlemen whose case is being presented here and without detracting in the least from their qualifications. I understand that it is also suggested that the pilots know more about depth of water. Anyone knows that a man operating a coasting vessel has to familiarize himself with conditions as to depth of water, and most coastwise vessels are of light draft anyway. Notwithstanding that my deskmate urges it so strongly, I have emphatically to record my sincere protest against any extension of this compulsory pilotage feature, and any further imposition of an increased burden on the coal trade of Nova Scotia.

I wish first of all to thank the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) for what he has said in regard to this matter. As he has pointed out, since confederation we have never had compulsory pilotage below Quebec, and we do not intend to have it now. I would also point out that these pilots are employed practically seven months of the year and are idle the remaining five. They are among the best paid classes of labour in this country, and they ought to be jolly well satisfied with their positions.
I admit, sir, with the two hon. members who have just preceded me in this debate, that since Confederation pilotage is not compulsory between Quebec and Father Point for vessels of Eastern Canada.
Speak in English, if you wish the majority of the house to listen to you. You can speak in English quite as well as in French.

I am aware of that.

However, by section 338, there was added, to the provinces already exempted from pilotage, the province of Ontario. The danger does not arise from vessels coming from the maritime

provinces but from those which do coastal trade on the Great Lakes and are ignorant of the regulations affecting navigation on the St. Lawrence river. Therefore, our objections- and I think that they are those of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain)-are not directed so much against vessels in the lower St. Lawrence as against those coming from the upper St. Lawrence river. Therefore, the act should be amended in such a way as to not make pilotage compulsory for vessels of the maritime provinces, but only for those of the upper St. Lawrence river.

If I may add a word, I think that the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency has struck the nail on the head. It is not so much the vessels of the maritime provinces which are a source of danger, because those who steer them are excellent navigators, but the danger lies with the vessels coming from the Great Lakes. Their captains contend that, after a few trips in the lower St. Lawrence and having called at certain ports, they are able to enter and leave such ports and, moreover, they are as competent as pilots, navigators and captains of the lower St. Lawrence river. I contend that such is not the case. I admit that, in some instances, the captains and pilots of the maritime provinces may be as well qualified as those who pilot the vessels from Father Point to Quebec; but where the difference lies is that vessels from the Great Lakes, which navigate under different conditions are unable, relying only on those who man them, to acquire sufficient knowledge of those waters to safely steer the vessels under their charge and prevent all accidents and damages which they are liable to meet on their course.
According to the information I have furnished the house, a moment ago, in almost every accident, the vessels had no pilot on board. I think, sir, it is not asking too much, and such an amendment should be conceded to us.

The amendment is that subsection 1 of section 2 be deleted and that subsection 2 be renumbered subsection 1, and that there be inserted as subsection 2 the following:
"Agreement with the crew" has the meaning as indicated in section 163 of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I would like in a few words to explain the reason for the amendment. The definition of "the admiralty" was in the bill before it was amended, because the word "admiralty" appeared in certain clauses of it. When the bill was amended in the other house, the word "admiralty" disappeared from the sections, but the definition remained, in order to make no change to the numbering of all the definitions, one hundred and thirteen in number. As some of those definitions are referred to in a large number of clauses by their number, corrections would have to be made in a large number of clauses, and so they thought they should leave that definition because it was of no importance whatever. But I think it is better to delete this definition and insert the one I have just read defining the words "agreement with the crew." In this way there will be no change in the numbering of the definitions.

I am sure I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Marine and anybody else connected with this bill, whether it be the
government or somebody else, have come to the conclusion after perusing this legislation that as I suggested a fortnight ago no reference is made in it to the definition that-
"The Admiralty" means the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom for the time being, or the commissioner for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom.
It is all very well for the minister after I suggested this a fortnight ago to say now that he is willing to cut out this subclause. This proves conclusively that the whole biil has never been properly considered by the ministry or parliament or this definition would never have been inserted. Why should a Canadian bill, a bill introduced in this parliament, whether in another place or here, refer to the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom? This proves conclusively that somebody fell down on the job. The minister this afternoon was very careful to tell us about what wonderful officials he had in the Marine department; but I say that the officials are not worth their salt or they would never have allowed the minister to come before parliament and be placed in the embarrassing position into which he has been put in the last fortnight and especially to-night when he had to admit on the floor of the house that in the 497 pages of this bill there is no reference to the Lord High Admiral or the commissioner for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom.
The minister, I suppose on the advice of his officials, has moved that a certain clause take the place of this one. That is not a reasonable clause to insert there and just at this juncture I will suggest a better one. The minister must admit that these subclauses are inserted alphabetically. Let me explain what I mean. The first definition is "the admiralty-Ad. The next is "Admiralty Court"; the next "Board", and it goes on A, B, C. The minister wants to insert in place of the definition of "The Admiralty" under A, something about seamen. If he wants to justify his officials and justify his high priced lawyers who for two years have been sweating over this bill and making a mess of things; if he wants to justify the nineteen gentlemen in another place who never saw salt water; if he wants to justify anybody, let me suggest to him that instead of the definition about the seamen and instead of the definition of "The Admiralty", he insert a definition of "this act". I am doing this just now without consulting a solicitor or anybody learned in the law. Perhaps the chairman will help me out because he is one of the most
Canada Shipping Act

eminent lawyers in Nova Scotia. Instead of putting in this foolish clause about seamen, which is entirely out of order because all these definitions are inserted alphabetically, let him make this subclause 1 of clause 2 read: " 'This act' means an act respecting shipping''. That will get the minister out of the hole and his officials out of the mess they are in and bring, them back again sailing in clear water. Let the minister stop this talk about seamen because we must have a certain method of procedure in regard to this bill. Will he accept the suggestion from me that instead of inserting a clause which means nothing at all he put in the marginal note of subclause 1 the words "this act" and then go on to say:
(1)	"This act" means an act respecting shipping.
That covers the clauses of Bill E and is much better than the amendment he moved, although I presume his officials have been sweating for ten days in an endeavour to find something to take the place of this subclause with regard to the admiralty and the Lord High Admiral, which should never have been in the bill in the first place if the minister had been properly advised, and if his officials had been the proper ones they would have never allowed this to come before parliament, thus placing the minister in the embarrassing position in which he has found himself in the last fortnight.
Was there any reference to the admiralty or the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom in any of the clauses of the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Not in the bill as
amended.

The only reason I am asking this is because the bill was submitted to us with that definition in the interpretation clause. There must have been some reason for putting that in. Like my confrere, the hon. member for Antigonish-Guy^borough,
I am much surprised; after a bill had been considered for practically the w'hole session before the other house, had been studied there last year also and had been studied as extensively as that the minister will readily admit it is most remarkable that in the last minutes before this bill is to be adopted we are told it is better that we should eliminate that clause and replace it by another. Surely the minister, whom I know to be a shrewd lawyer, who has a high standing at the bar, who was our batonnier and of whom we are 
all ptraud, will admit that we have some justification for our criticism of the bill.

If this amendment carries, it will practically complete the bill 'and I think it does away with subclause 1. Before this happens, as it affects the engagement of seamen, let me make a last appeal to the minister regarding a clause-

All right.

I must ask the minister now
to take time to consider what I have suggested. If he is going to delete this subsection 1 which refers to the admiralty and which he admits should never have been in this bill, he should put in some clause which relates specifically to this part of the bill. The amendment the minister has offered is not necessary.

Because it is not, that is the reason. I say that it would be much better if the minister would take my suggestion-

And in this bill there is no
reference to the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom. If we had a lord high admiral of Canada I could understand it and would not object, but it refers to the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom for the time being or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom. If those high-priced lawyers and the officials of the marine department and everyone who has been associated with the minister made this mistake in the very first subsection of this bill, what must we expect from the 497 pages of it? The minister wants to delete this *section and put in another one with regard to seamen. I say that is not in order. What we put in this subsection should conform to
