the alphabetical arrangement of these interpretation clauses. The minister's amendment does not fit in alphabetically. He tries to persuade us that he is saving money by taking out this section and making subsection 2 subsection 1 and so on instead of reprinting the bill. But he is not doing that at all. All he is doing is trying to save the face of either the hon. gentlemen in another house, or the high priced lawyers the minister had to deal with this bill, or some of his officials. My suggestion is that the minister's amendment should not be carried in order to save the face of those lawyers or those officials, but that clause 1 of section 2 should refer to this bill. It is a very simple thing; just say that this act means an act respecting shipping as contained in Bill E.
I submit that it is much better than the minister's amendment. I am sure his official must have stayed up nights trying to find something to take the place of this foolish reference to the Lord High Admiral and the commissioners for the time being executing that office in the old country.

It is just to fill in a
gap.

The minister's officials have
sweated over this and the minister himself has got grey-headed over it, and now he takes out the admiralty and instead of proceeding in the order of A, B, C, D, he is putting in its place an interpretation regarding seamen which should appear at about subsection 90. The minister surely should accept my suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, may I
ask the indulgence of the committee for a few minutes while I try to deal with my hon. friend the Presbyterian elder from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff)? This afternoon my hon. friend although entirely out of order continued to speak for some considerable time. When his attention was called to the fact that he was out of order he said that if allowed to continue he would not speak again during this day. I am reminded of a story concerning a man in the old country who was elected an elder of the church. On his way home he saw his cow in the field and he said to her: "Betty, ye are no' a common coo the noo; ye are nothin' less than an elder's coo." Now my hon. friend has recently been elected an elder of the Presbyterian church of his home town, and I submit in view of that he ought to be a little more careful in regard to keeping promises he makes, particularly in this honourable house.
Shall the amendment carry?

No, Mr. Chairman, it cannot
carry in view of what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) has said. There is one principle in the Presbyterian church which requires that a man must be honest and sincere in his convictions. My hon. friend and I agree, except in this, that my hon. friend, who now occupies the chair of the Prime Minister-[DOT]
No, you are wrong.

Well, the chair of the Minister of Justice. I am sure I would be delighted to see him move up there; in fact I would like to see him move up into the other house. The other night my hon. friend was the greatest critic of this bill. He told us that the phraseology of certain sections was absolutely wrong. Yet this afternoon and tonight as a sheep before her shearers is dumb so my hon. friend, openeth not his mouth. Why? Because the Prime Minister or some other influence or magnet has drawn him over into the seat of the Minister of Justice and now he tries to tell us that this bill should go through. My hon. friend knows* very well that this bill is all wrong. He knows that there are clauses in it which he as a shipping man-and he knows a great deal more about shipping than I do-could not approve. He knows that Part II should be changed; he knows that this bill should not go through the house hurriedly-
Stick to your promise.

That is not quite fair. I
admit that perhaps I have fallen from grace, but my hon. friend has fallen a number of times even if he is now sitting by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who of course knows more about grace than either my hon. friend or I. I want to say to my hon. friend that this is a very important matter, and he knows it, a matter in which every man who goes down to the sea in ships is interested. The other day when I called the attention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice and the attention of this committee to the fact that there is no mention of the Lord High Admiral in this bill, no mention of the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom, in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister is perhaps better informed and has a greater memory than any other man in this parliament, yet he could not find in the 497 pages, the 719 clauses, or the schedules of this bill where the Lord High Admiral and the commissioners for the time being for executing his office are mentioned. He tried to find it, and I appreciate his effort, but to-night we have the minister
Canada Shipping Act

admitting that there is no such thing in the bill. Why should there be? This is a bill of the Canadian parliament; we have no lord high admiral; we have no commissioners of the admiralty in this country. It just proves conclusively that this whole bill has been badly drawn. In spite of the fact that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine had this man Griffin come from Vancouver at $100 a day, just as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has a $150 a day man in this other committee of his and has other lawyers at $100 and $50 a day-
Order, please. That has nothing whatever to do with the clause under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly am in order in discussing the motion of the minister that this subsection be deleted. I am giving reasons why this clause should never have appeared in the bill. In spite of the fact that high priced lawyers and officials of the Marine department have been worrying over this bill for the last two years, the lawyers inserted the clause in the first place. The minister told me a fortnight ago and told this house that he had read the bill, and yet he now wants to delete the clause, in spite of the fact that only a week ago the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice sat in their seats and looked over the bill, and could not find any clause or part of it in which the Lord High Admiral or the commissioners of the admiralty were mentioned. I say the amendment he has moved concerning seamen is not in place, and I suggest he should add a simple clause in order to conform with the alphabetical order of the bill. Hon. members will note that the definitions are indicated alphabetically. For instance, the first subsection deals with the admiralty, and then comes one dealing with the admiralty court. Then there is a subsection dealing with the definition of the word Board." Definitions follow in their alphabetical order, namely, C, D, E, F, G. But to-night the minister wants to make a statement about seamen in the first subsection. I suggest that in order to save his face, and in order to save the face of the government who paid out thousands of dollars to bring this conglomeration of nothing before parliament, the minister could insert in the clause the words " 'This act' means every clause in this bill E regarding shipping." I make this suggestion to the minister. I know he will not agree with it; he will take the advice of some official who does not know what he is talking about. Of course the minister will not take my advice, and I do not care whether 
he does or not. No doubt this bill will go through, because the Prime Minister is determined to push it through. It certainly is not a very great credit to anybody to put through a bill like this. The present bill will be passed as the first legislation based on the convention of a few years ago. All right, if the minister wishes the bill to pass, he may have it passed. But the men interested in shipping will wake up to-morrow morning and they will look at the amendment the minister is moving to-night, an amendment which is not even alphabetically correct, and express their disapproval. The minister admits there is no mention in the act about the admiralty or the commissioner. Why does he not put in the simple amendment I have suggested, and simply say, " 'This act' means every clause in this bill E regarding shipping."

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
On section 2, subsection 38-Home trade voyage.

I have one or two observations to make, because I believe section 120 passed when I was not in the chamber, and I may make some observations on this subsection. It has been brought to my attention that a change has been made in the description of a home trade voyage, and it is possible that some of the certificates of coastal captains may suffer thereby. I have discussed the matter with the assistant to the deputy minister who has given me some assurance in the matter, but I should like to have a definite statement from the minister who is piloting this bill through the House of Commons. I should like to know that those who have their certificates as coastal captains qualified to take ships up to the Labrador coast, or down to the Bermudas, will not be prevented from operating those boats. I have in mind the Clarke Steamship Company. I was told that with the description indicated the certificates would be issued to coastal captains with certain limitations. I should like to be properly posted. It may be that the law would apply only to the new certificates issued in future.
I notice that section 120 provides for a renewal at the expiration of the period of five years. My point is as to whether or not they will be renewed in accordance with the terms of the present legislation, or the terms of the act as it stood previously.
Mr. DURANL.EAU: That part of section 120 has been deleted.

It has been deleted?

Canada Shipping Act

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, the part limiting the life of the certificate to five years has been deleted. The certificates are not in any way affected by this bill. It affects only the future.
Do I understand that when old captains with coastal certificates come back and ask for renewals those certificates will be renewed in accordance with the terms which prevailed when they were issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
They have a life certificate. They do not need renewal, except in the event of loss of their certificate. I have an amendment to subsection 38 of section 2.
I move that the words, "north of the 60th parallel of north latitude or" be stricken out from lines 47 and 48, and that at line 49, after the word "latitude" the words "or through Bering strait" be added. The question as to the Hudson bay route has been raised. By the amendment, except on the west side, the limiting line to the north is deleted. On the west side the only limitation is that a home voyage boat could not pass through Bering strait.

If the minister can be so generous, why does he not make it the north pole? Why mention Bering strait? Certainly there is no necessity to make it Bering strait. Of course the minister would not accept my suggestion because he would not consider it proper. In moving this amendment, however, he admits that I called to his attention and the attention of the government the fact that there had been a mistake made in naming the sixtieth parallel. Now he comes along, and instead of accepting my suggestion of substituting the sixty-fifth parallel of north latitude, he mentions Bering strait. Why not go the whole distance? Canada owns the north pole; she owns all the territory north of Hudson bay. Why does the minister, on the advice of his officials I presume, not accept my suggestion? Oh, no, they could not do that, of course. That would be altogether too much to ask. That would be very humiliating to the minister and to the government. My suggestion was made to-day to increase the northern latitude to the sixty-fifth parallel, and I believe it is better than the Bering strait suggestion. Does the minister know where Bering strait is? How far north is Bering strait. What parallel is it in? Surely if any person has pluck enough to pilot a vessel to the north pole the minister should not expect him in a home voyage, to go no farther than Bering strait. Why not make it zero? Why say Bering strait? Why do
the officials talk about Bering strait? Will my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce look at the map, and if he does he will find that it does not affect the Pacific situation. It is surely much better to move the parallel from 65 to 70, or whatever it is. It just shows, Mr. Chairman, that the minister's officials are not advising him properly. I am going to ask the minister either to accept my suggestion and make it the sixty-fifth parallel or let this clause stand until tomorrow so that his advisers may advise him what is right. Why talk about Bering strait? The only thing a navigator knows is the parallels of latitude and longitude. What is the latitude in Bering strait, for instance? The minister is looking at the map. Will he please tell me-I have not a map before me-what is the latitude of Bering strait? We have now six men crowding around the minister looking to see what latitude Bering strait is in. Will the minister please tell the committee what latitude it is in? Why will not the minister accept my suggestion to move the parallel from sixty to sixty-five, which is the proper nautical way to do it. and that would make a voyage to Hudson bay a home-trade voyage? But the minister on the advice of some official in his department, who has no doubt stayed up nights trying to give advice, says that he is going to make this home-trade voyage to Bering strait. Why does he not accept my suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Just a word of explanation. The question of the Hudson bay voyage was raised in this house and we thought we could allow' a voyage on the Hudson bay route as a home-trade vovage, under regulations passed by order in council. The parallel sixty has been eliminated because there is no other voyage to the north on the Atlantic side, and we did not see any reason why we should limit a voyage on the Atlantic side to the sixty-fifth parallel. But on the west coast, after considering the matter, a ship going through Bering strait and as far as the Mackenzie river, let us say, would have to go across deep water, across the sea, and then it becomes a foreign voyage where the hazards of navigation are greater. That is why the limitation on the home voyage on the we'stern coast is the passage of Bering strait. I do not think my hon. friend can have any objection to that, for he knows perfectly well that Bering strait is between the sixtieth and seventieth parallels, and if he will read the amendment I am sure he will find it is quite proper under the circumstances.

Canada Shipping Act

The minister admits that I am right. He says that Bering strait is between north parallels sixty-4ive and seventy. Why then does he not accept my suggestion to make the parallel sixty-five both on the west coast and on the east coast? Why name Bering strait? If I want to leave Nova Scotia and go to the north pole I will go further than the sixty-fifth north parallel.
The minister says that the Mackenzie river voyage would !be a foreign voyage. Surely he does not mean that. No voyage in Canada, and of course the Mackenzie river is in Canada, is a foreign voyage. The minister is being badly advised. I say that all he has to do is to accept my suggestion. I am the one who brought it up, because, due, I will not say to the stupidity of the lawyers who drafted this bill, but to lack of knowledge of the members of the committee in the other house, they deliberately in the clause which we have to consider in this bill limited the home-trade voyage to the sixtieth parallel of north latitude. That means that a voyage to the Hudson bay would not be a home-trade voyage. Once you get fifty miles away from cape Chidley on the Labrador coast you are outside of the home-trade limits, and you are on a foreign voyage. The hon. member for Nelson agreed with me in that because he immediately asked the minister that this clause should stand for further consideration. Let us be fair about this thing. Why should we not make this clause read in a proper manner? Why should we say Bering strait? The suggestion I made to the minister this afternoon was that the home-trade voyage should include Canada, the United States, Mexico, the territory of Alaska, Newfoundland, Labrador, St. Pierre and Miquelon and the West Indies, in the course of which a ship does not go north of the sixty-fifth parallel of north latitude. No ship wants to go north of that, and the minister admits that Bering strait is within that definition. Why does the minister not accept the suggestion I made? Surely he must admit that I have a little knowledge of marine matters. I do not want to embarrass the minister. I am trying to help him. But just because the officials of his department have made a mess of this thing the minister will! not admit that a mistake has teen made. I say that it is not right for him to come in and move this amendment. He admits that the clause is wrong because he wants to amend it, and I say that he should accept my amendment and that the north latitude should go to the sixty-[Mr. Duranleau.j
fifth degree, and so far as the south latitude is concerned instead of going to cape Hatteras it should go down to British Guiana which is five degrees north of the equator.
I am simply trying to be fair, Mr. Chairman. The minister must admit that I have no axe to grind. There is no politics in this thing, because if there were, I would simply let the bill go through holus bolus and then go out and say to every mariner in this country that this bill is a mess, and I would show them why it is wrong. All I am trying to do is to show the minister that this clause drawn up by somebody, I do not know whether it was his officials in the department or someone else, is all wrong.
Let me draw the attention of the committee to the definition of a coasting voyage under the old act. A coasting voyage is being changed by this bill to a home-trade voyage. Now under the definition of a coasting voyage under the old act a ship could go on a coasting voyage down as far as Buenos Aires. But under a home-trade voyage, where does the minister want a ship to go? Not to Buenos Aires, not to Pernambuco, not to British Guiana, not to the British West Indies, not to Bermuda-no. Where? To cape Hatteras. Is that fair? Why this distinction? What does it mean?
I call the attention of the Minister of Railways particularly to this matter because the hon. gentleman wants the Canadian merchant marine and the national steamships to make money, and I say to him and to the Minister of Marine and to this committee that this clause, instead of reading the thirty-sixth north latitude, which is cape Hatteras, should read the fifth north, which includes the West Indies and British Guiana. Why does not the minister accept my suggestion? I do not want to talk all the time about this thing, but surely the minister, instead of taking the advice of his officials who stayed awake nights trying to give him advice, should admit the reasonableness of my argument. Let the home-trade voyage go down to British Guiana where the Canadian National steamships go and where the vessels from Nova Scotia go. Why say that they can go only as far as cape Hatteras? Whoever heard tell of a Nova Scotia vessel going to cape Hatteras? She may pass the cape but she does not stop there. However, a vessel may go to British Guiana or to the Barbadoes or to St. Kitts or Bermuda. In order to justify the position taken by some of his officials the minister refuses to accept my

Canada Shipping Act
suggestion. I am not talking politics, I am talking business when I say that a ship has a proper right to be considered on a home-trade voyage when she leaves Vancouver to go down the western coast to Panama, then through the canal and up to Halifax. Instead of referring to the Bering strait, which does not mean anything, the minister should use the sailor's term of latitude. I contend that the sixty-fifth degree will meet the objection raised by the hon. member for New Westminster. Under the section as it now is no ship could go into Hudson bay on a home-trade voyage; it would have to be a foreign voyage. Let the minister be fair and decent about this thing. He should not mind his officials. I admit that they have made mistakes, but this parliament is more important than the officials of the Department of Marine. I say to the minister that he should adopt the suggestions which I gave this afternoon. Such a voyage should be permitted to the sixty-fifth parallel of north latitude and down to the fifth. This would mean that a ship could go the Hudson bay and down as far as British Guiana. Such an amendment would be in the interests of the seamen and the shipping of this country.

Does the minister
intend to amend subsection 38?

I should like the minister to
tell us what led him to make such a substantial change in the coasting area allowed to this class of certificate.
